sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: The EQ-5D-5L is a multi-attribute utility instrument recommended by many health technology assessment agencies. This study aimed to develop an EQ-5D-5L value set for Singapore.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A ‘lite’ version of the EuroQol Research Foundation’s EQ-5D-5L valuation protocol, which was designed to value a total of 91 health states using a composite time trade-off (cTTO) method, was followed. Five hundred members of the general public in Singapore were quota-sampled and invited to a personal interview face-to-face or via Zoom. All participants completed 20 cTTO tasks administered using the EuroQol Valuation Technology (EQ-VT) program. Cross-validation analysis was performed to identify the best-performing model for estimating the values of all the 3,125 EQ-5D-5L health states.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A 20-parameter main-effects model with two two-way interaction terms outperformed other models in the cross-validation analysis. The value set estimated using this model ranges from − 0.851 (for state 55555) to 1.000 (for state 11111), with pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression dimensions associated with the greatest disutility.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: We developed an EQ-5D-5L value set based on the health preferences of Singaporeans. We recommend EQ-5D-5L users in Singapore to use this value set and encourage a more systematic and dedicated methodological effort to understand interaction effects and potential non-linearities in the valuation of multi-attribute health descriptive systems.

sec.title: Supplementary Information
sec.p: The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s40273-025-01519-7.

tr.td: We developed the first 5-level EQ-5D (EQ-5D-5L) value set for Singapore and codes for using prevailing statistical software programs to generate the values from survey data.
A 20-parameter main-effects model with two two-way interaction terms was chosen to represent the preferences of the Singaporean general public for EQ-5D-5L health states.

As the local EQ-5D-3L values differ significantly from the EQ-5D-5L values, it is recommended to score EQ-5D-3L data using the EQ-5D-5L value set especially for the purpose of economic evaluation of new health technologies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The EQ-5D-5L [1] is currently one of the most commonly utilized multi-attribute utility instruments for calculating quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) in cost-utility analysis (CUA). Like its predecessor, the 3-level EQ-5D (EQ-5D-3L) [2], it classifies an individual’s health status using five dimensions, namely, mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression; however, EQ-5D-5L describes each dimension with five functional levels, namely, no, slight, moderate, severe, and extreme problems or unable to perform the relevant activities. This system defines a total of 3,125 unique health states, allowing for a more nuanced description of health outcomes. Studies have confirmed that EQ-5D-5L has superior measurement properties compared to EQ-5D-3L [3, 4]. To estimate QALYs, the values for all the EQ-5D-5L health states, known as a 'value set', must be established. Following the recommendations of methodological guidelines for CUA, e.g. [5], many countries have developed their own EQ-5D-5L value sets, with more expected to follow [6]. Country-specific value sets are preferred due to significant differences in preferences for EQ-5D health states observed between different populations [7–9].

EQ-5D-3L was first introduced into Singapore in 2003 [10, 11]. With increasing evidence for its good psychometric properties in the local populations [12–15], EQ-5D-3L has gained substantial use over the years as a generic health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measure in both clinical research and practice as well as value-based care. It has also been widely used to collect HRQoL data for economic evaluation in Singapore, particularly after a local EQ-5D-3L value set was established in 2014 [16]. EQ-5D-5L was introduced into Singapore in 2015 [17, 18], and as in other countries, has demonstrated superior measurement properties compared to EQ-5D-3L in local populations [19, 20].

This study aimed to develop an EQ-5D-5L value set for Singapore, where economic evaluation has been formally employed to inform reimbursement and adoption decisions for new health technologies and QALY is considered the most appropriate measure of health benefit [21].

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The study followed a ‘lite’ version of the EuroQol’s EQ-5D-5L valuation protocol [22] and used the latest available version of EuroQol Valuation Technology (EQ-VT) (version 2.1) [23–25], a computer-assisted personal interviewing program, to collect preferences data from a sample of the general adult population in Singapore. The study received approval from the Institutional Review Board of the National University of Singapore (NUS-IRB-2022-598).

sec.title: The ‘Lite’ EQ-5D-5L Valuation Protocol
sec.p: This ‘lite’ EQ-5D-5L valuation protocol was first used in an EQ-5D-5L valuation study in Uganda [22]. It was developed for use when recruiting a large general population sample is either infeasible or very expensive. Different from the standard protocol, the ‘lite’ protocol requires a sample size of only 500 individuals and includes only composite time trade-off (cTTO) valuation tasks. However, each individual needs to complete 20 cTTO tasks in contrast to 10 cTTO tasks per individual in standard EQ-5D-5L valuation studies. Five blocks of 20 health states were generated from the 10 blocks of health states (each comprising 55555) used in the standard protocol by pairing the blocks and then replacing one of the two 55555 states in each combined block with one of the five second-poorest health states (i.e. 45555, 54555, 55455, 55545, and 55554). As a result, a total of 91 health states (i.e. 86 states from the standard protocol plus the five second-poorest states) were included for valuation in the ‘lite’ protocol. Each participant in our study was randomly assigned to one of the five health-state blocks for valuation. As the ‘lite’ protocol was proven to be feasible and we had limited resources, we elected to use this new protocol in the current valuation study, which was approved by the EuroQol Research Foundation.

sec.title: Sampling and Recruitment
sec.p: Singapore is a multi-ethnic society comprising primarily Chinese, Malay, and Indian communities, with 87% of the population being literate in either English or Chinese [26]. We used a quota sampling method to ensure the distributions of age, sex, ethnicity, and education of the study sample resemble those reported for the Singapore 2021/2022 population [27, 28].

Participants were initially recruited from the Singapore Multi-Ethnic Cohort study, which comprised more than 20,000 residents, and is maintained by the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health at the National University of Singapore [29, 30]. As quotas for certain minority groups could not be filled, we also recruited additional participants using social media advertisements. In collaboration with administrators of the cohort study and local online communities, we invited potentially eligible individuals to register online, assessed their eligibility, and then invited eligible individuals to fill preset quotas. The inclusion criteria for the study were as follows: (1) individuals aged 21 years or older, which is the legal age of adulthood in Singapore; (2) able to read and communicate in either English or Chinese; and (3) physically and mentally capable of completing an interview, either in-person or via Zoom. The exclusion criterion was prior participation in an EQ-VT study. Participation in the study was voluntary, and participants were compensated with SGD40 (approximately US$30).

sec.title: Data Collection
sec.p: Each eligible participant was invited to a computer-assisted interview using the EQ-VT program. The interviews were conducted either face-to-face or via video conferencing. While the EQ-VT program was designed for in-person interviews, it was adapted for video conferencing during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic [31–33] and comparative studies showed that there were no significant differences in data collected using face-to-face or video-conferencing interviews [33, 34]. As individual preferences and practical concerns may play a role in study participation, both modes of administration were offered to maximize inclusion. The interviews were structured into four sections: Section 1 introduced the study, Section 2 captured participants' demographics and health status via the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire, Section 3 involved 20 cTTO valuation tasks preceded by a tutorial using an 'in wheelchair' example and three practices, and Section 4 assessed participants’ considerations behind their choices in the cTTO tasks using both closed-ended and open-ended questions.

All interviews were conducted by five research staff members and graduate students from the National University of Singapore who had recently conducted EQ-VT interviews as part of a multi-country EQ-5D-Y valuation study. Throughout the data collection period, interviewers’ performance was monitored as part of a standard quality control process developed by the EuroQol Group [35]. Specifically, two experienced data quality specialists periodically evaluated collected data and provided individualized feedback to interviewers. The evaluation was focused on potential quality issues including (1) less than 3 minutes spent explaining the wheelchair example, (2) failure to demonstrate the worse-than-dead element in the wheelchair example, (3) value for the ‘55555’ health state higher than any other value by 0.5 points, and (4) less than 5 minutes spent completing all the cTTO tasks.

sec.title: Valuation Procedure
sec.p: The cTTO approach combines the conventional time trade-off (TTO) (i.e. 10 years in an EQ-5D state) for valuing health states considered better than dead (BTD) and the lead-time TTO (i.e. 10 years in full health followed by 10 years in an EQ-5D state) for health states considered worse than dead (WTD). For each health state to be valued, respondents were first asked their preference between living in full health for 10 years and living in this state for 10 years. The length of time lived in full health varied each time by 1 or 0.5 years until the two options were indifferent to respondents. When respondents’ preferences indicated that a state was WTD (i.e. preferring 0 years in full health or ‘die now’ to living in the health state for 10 years followed by death), they were introduced into the lead-time TTO to choose between 10 years of full health (life A) and 10 years of full health followed by 10 years in the health state that is valued (life B). The number of years in life A was varied until indifference or 0 years was reached. Thus, a total of 41 unique values between 1 and − 1 could be expressed.

sec.title: Data Analysis
sec.p: Our data analysis consisted of four stages: data selection, model construction, model evaluation, and value set estimation.

sec.title: Data Selection
sec.p: We examined individual-level cTTO data and excluded respondents who valued all 20 health states as − 1 or whose values increased with health-state severity. Such respondents would be considered as failing to understand the valuation tasks.

sec.title: Model Construction
sec.p: Based on the design of recent EQ-5D valuation studies that we conducted or participated in [36–40], we constructed and tested a total of six tobit regression models in which the individual disutility value (i.e. 1 minus cTTO value) was regressed on the dimensional characteristics of valued health states. Tobit modelling was used because the cTTO values were censored at − 1.0. To ensure the model-predicted cTTO value for the full health state (i.e. 11111) was 1.0, the tested models did not include an intercept. The six models were as follows: (1) the conventional 20-parameter main-effects-only model (ADD20); (2) the 20-parameter model with two-way interaction terms (ADD20-I); (3) the 20-parameter model with a power function (ADD20-P); (4) the eight-parameter cross-attribute level effects (CALE) [41] model; (5) the CALE model with two-way interaction terms (CALE-I); and (6) the CALE model with a power function (CALE-P).

sec.title: Model Evaluation
sec.p: Next, we used a cross-validation procedure to evaluate the models. Specifically, we used data from four of the five blocks of health states to estimate the models and used the remaining block to evaluate their performance. We repeated this analysis five times so that each health-state block was used for the purpose of validation. In each iteration, we examined (1) the significance and logical consistency of estimated model coefficients and (2) the out-of-sample prediction accuracy in terms of root mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). The averaged RMSE, MAE, and ICC from the five iterations were used to evaluate prediction accuracy of the tested models. For calculating RMSE, MAE, and ICC in each iteration, we used censoring-adjusted mean cTTO values of the 20 health states in the block for validation and the values predicted by the tested models. We chose to use censoring-adjusted means instead of observed means because the cTTO values were censored at − 1. To adjust for the censoring, we fitted the observed cTTO values of each health state consecutively into a tobit model with only the intercept term. As some of the 10 interaction terms might be insignificant, we used the entire sample and a backward selection method to identify significant interaction terms and included only those interaction terms in the cross-validation analysis. All the six model specifications were estimated with and without the heteroskedasticity of the cTTO data being accounted for.

sec.title: Value Set Estimation
sec.p: Finally, all the models were estimated using the entire dataset. Moreover, all the value sets were assessed for their logical consistency, namely, whether the predicted value for a health state is higher than the predicted value for another health state when the former is better than the latter according to their characteristics. This logical consistency was examined for a total of 759,375 pairs of EQ-5D-5L health states. All models were fitted using a non-linear mixed effects function from the xreg package (available at: www.github.com/intelligentaccident/xreg). A p value of less than 0.05 was adopted as the threshold for statistical significance in all analyses.

sec.title: Results
sec.p:
Data were collected between November 2023 and April 2024. A total of 533 eligible individuals from the cohort study and online communities registered for participation. Of these, 500 individuals were successfully recruited and interviewed, resulting in a response rate of 93.8%. The participants had a mean age of 48.1 years (standard deviation 16.6). The majority were of Chinese ethnicity (76.8%), 49.8% were females, and 46.6% held at least a diploma. There were no missing values for the cTTO tasks, and no respondents were excluded from the study based on pre-defined exclusion criteria. The cTTO values were distributed across the scale from − 1 to 1, with spikes at − 1 (16.1%) and 1 (14.3%), and minor spikes at 0 (5.4%) and 0.5 (7.5%) (Fig. 1).Fig. 1
Distribution of observed composite time trade-off (cTTO) values

Only two interaction terms (i.e. mobility × anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort × anxiety/depression) were significant when data from the entire sample was fitted to ADD20-I and CALE-I. In the cross-validation analysis, coefficients for all main-effect and interaction terms as well as the power function parameter were statistically significant in all or most of the iterations.

In cross-validation analysis, all six model specifications performed better when heteroskedasticity in cTTO data was accounted for (Table 3). Among all models tested, the ADD20-I model demonstrated the best performance, and the advantage was greater when data heteroskedasticity was accounted for (RMSE 0.0782; MAE 0.0598; ICC 0.9883). When heteroskedasticity was accounted for, the second best performed model was CALE-I, followed by the two power function models (ADD20-P and CALE-P) and the two main-effects models (ADD20 and CALE) (Table 3). Using the best-performed ADD20-I, which accounts for heteroskedasticity, approximately 60% of the values (N = 1,862) were between 0 and 1; the lowest and second highest values were − 0.851 and 0.956, respectively. Fig. 2 shows the distribution of the predicted values for the 3,125 states in relation to the mean cTTO values of the 91 valued states after adjustment for censoring at − 1. The full value set for all 3,125 health states is available in Excel format as supplementary data (Online Resource 1; see the electronic supplementary material). Figure 3 shows that this value set is substantially different from the ‘mapped’ EQ-5D-5L value set for Singapore, which is generated by first mapping EQ-5D-5L health states to EQ-5D-3L health states using a recommended mapping function [43] and then applying the local EQ-5D-3L value set [16].Fig. 2

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: To our knowledge, it is the first EQ-5D-5L value set estimated using a model that includes between-dimension interaction terms. Previous EQ-5D-5L valuation studies did not model interactions between dimensions because a total of 160 such interactions can be specified using the 20 dummy-coded main effects. It is challenging to model those interactions using data collected under the EQ-VT protocol, which is specifically designed for estimating the 20-parameter main-effects model. Nevertheless, we applied a novel yet simple approach that captured all possible between-dimension interactions with only 10 terms, making it feasible to model them in EQ-VT studies. Although our specifications were based on untested assumptions, emerging evidence on interactions between EQ-5D dimensions in valuation studies highlights the importance of considering models beyond the basic main-effects model when estimating EQ-5D value sets [42, 44]. Indeed, our study showed that interaction terms improved model prediction when added to the 20-parameter main-effects model or the eight-parameter CALE model (a variant of the main-effects model). The power function models also outperformed the main-effects models, further suggesting that the linearity assumption inherent in the main-effects model may not be optimal. The superior performance of interaction models over power function models may be attributed to their dimension-specific non-linearity between health problems and preferences.

Our study revealed a concave rather than a convex relationship between health problems and preferences, suggesting that the disutility of compounded or cooccurred health problems of different types was lower than the sum of the disutility of the individual health problems. Similarly, several valuation studies found significant interactions between EQ-5D dimensions [42, 44, 45] and that cooccurrence of health problems mitigated the overall disutility, though the interactions occurred to different health dimensions in different studies. These findings suggest that EQ-5D health dimensions are more likely to be complementary (i.e. functions synergizing with each other) than substitutive (i.e. functions replacing each other) in achieving functions important to respondents.

The value set we estimated in this study differs from the EQ-5D-3L value set for Singapore in several aspects. First, the current values are higher. For example, the proportion of the − 1 value in the current and the previous valuation studies is 16% and approximately 30%, respectively. Second, the relative importance of the health dimensions between the two value sets are very different. For example, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression are the two most important dimensions in the current value set, whereas those are the least important dimensions in the previous value set. The change in the relative importance of health dimensions from the previous study to the current study could reflect a real change in health preferences of the Singapore population in the past decade. Such change is possible due to the rapidly aging Singapore population and the COVID-19 pandemic. For example, the lockdown experience might have intensified people’s perception of mental health issues such as anxiety. The differences in EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L values could be partially due to differences in the descriptors used by the two descriptive systems. Specifically, the worst level of mobility is described as ‘confined to bed’ in EQ-5D-3L and ‘unable to walk about’ in EQ-5D-5L. While the true reasons for the differences between the value sets cannot be confirmed, the new EQ-5D-5L value set is estimated using validated data collection procedures and contemporary health preferences and therefore is superior to the existing EQ-5D-3L value set. Because of the differences between the two local EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L value sets, we recommend users of the EQ-5D-3L in Singapore map their data to the EQ-5D-5L descriptive system, for example, by using the algorithm developed by van Hout and Shaw [46], and then apply the EQ-5D-5L value set developed in the present study. We have developed a 3L-to-5L crosswalk calculator, which is available from Online Resource 5.

Our study may have important implications for future EQ-5D-5L valuation studies. First, the ‘lite’ valuation protocol we used appears to be a feasible option when there are resource or time constraints for data collection. The smaller sample size recommended by the ‘lite’ protocol, however, may reduce the precision of resultant value sets. Therefore, investigators should use the standard protocol whenever possible. Second, future studies should consider the use of designs that allow certain forms of cross-validation. A convenient strategy is to partition valuation data into two datasets by block and use one dataset to estimate models and the other dataset to evaluate model prediction, like what we did in this study. If the evaluation is based on performance in in-sample prediction, overfitted models may prevail. Previous studies have demonstrated the usefulness of cross-validation analysis in identifying better models for EQ-5D-5L values [39, 41, 47]. Third, we advocate for updates to valuation study designs that enable the evaluation of a broader range of models, particularly interaction models. This should also be accompanied by more systematic and dedicated methodological efforts to explore potential non-linearities between health problems and preferences. In addition to the interaction model and power function model tested in this study, emerging approaches such as the recently published interaction model using an optimal scaling method [44] also warrant evaluation. The assessment and estimation of these models will benefit from larger designs incorporating a greater number of health states.

While modelling interactions is a strength, our study is limited by the data we modelled. Following the ‘lite’ EQ-VT protocol, which was designed for estimating the 20-parameter main-effects model, we only valued 91 health states. These data may have limited our ability to detect all potentially significant interactions. Moreover, we assumed the main effects are continuous when constructing the interaction terms. As a result, our models may have been constrained in fully capturing the interaction effects. Nevertheless, the interaction models outperformed the main-effects models in cross-validation, supporting the pragmatic approach we chose to use. Another limitation of this study is suboptimal representativeness of the study sample. Due to limited resources, study participants were mainly recruited from active members of a large cohort for studying the risk factors of chronic health conditions. It is possible that the participants have different health preferences compared to other local residents. Moreover, although we performed quota sampling for recruitment, our study sample was not entirely representative of the target population because less educated and ethnic minority groups were slightly underrepresented. Nevertheless, there were generally no significant differences in cTTO values derived from different education or ethnic groups (Online Resource 6; see the electronic supplementary material). Lastly, our study employed two interview modes (i.e. in-person and via Zoom). We offered both interview options to participants, allowing them to choose based on their preferences, which helped minimise recruitment bias. The use of two interview modes might have introduced systematic differences into the cTTO data. Nevertheless, we found no evidence of such differences when comparing data derived from the two interview modes (Online Resource 7).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this study, we developed an EQ-5D-5L value set using a ‘lite’ valuation protocol and the health preferences of Singaporeans. This value set allows calculation of QALYs using locally collected EQ-5D-5L data for economic evaluation in the local setting. For the convenience of users, we have developed R, Stata, and SPSS code, along with a calculator for deriving EQ-5D-5L index scores using this value set (Online Resources 2–5; see the electronic supplementary material). We encourage future valuation studies to investigate potential interactions between health dimensions when modelling multi-attribute health preferences, ideally using methodologically robust study designs.
